outline_action: Use this study to document the current standard of plasma-based metabolomic profiling in ICI trials and to highlight the absence of paired intratumoral metabolite data in major cohorts. Cite the inosine-UBA6 mechanism as a rationale for why intratumoral measurement would be valuable (since the target is tumor-intrinsic). Search for additional studies that specifically performed metabolomics on resected human tumor biopsies paired with plasma/fecal samples to address the TME quantification gap.
remaining_gap: This study does not report direct quantification of inosine or other metabolites within human tumor tissue (TME); measurements were restricted to plasma in humans and tumor tissue in mice. There is no comparison of human intratumoral metabolite concentrations versus fecal or plasma samples in ICI-treated patients. The specific methodology for human TME metabolite extraction and quantification remains unaddressed in this text.
useful_material: This study utilized Matrix-Assisted Laser Desorption/Ionization mass spectrometry imaging (MALDI-MSI) to perform in situ metabolite quantification in paired human non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) tumor and normal tissue (n=15). The authors reported significantly higher levels of UMP, AMP, and ADP in tumor tissue compared to normal tissue, while metabolites downstream of adenosine, specifically adenine and inosine, showed no significant differences. This demonstrates the technical feasibility of directly quantifying specific metabolites, including inosine, within the human tumor microenvironment using mass spectrometry, which aligns with the methodological aspect of the gap question.
Human plasma metabolomics data from RCC patients (CheckMate 025 trial) treated with nivolumab, identifying inosine levels associated with overall survival.
Methodological detail on untargeted metabolomics using HPLC coupled with tripleTOF mass spectrometry on plasma samples.
Evidence linking gut microbiota depletion (antibiotics) to reduced inosine levels and compromised ICB efficacy in mouse models.
Clinical correlation of UBA6 protein expression (not metabolite) in human tumor tissues with ICB response.
Confirmation that inosine is a microbial-associated metabolite influencing ICI therapy outcomes.

The review explicitly confirms the methodological gap, stating that for most metabolites and delivery formats, validated models linking input to in-tissue exposure are lacking, and cancer-immunology use of biosensing/imaging tools is nascent.

It identifies specific techniques capable of direct quantification, including imaging mass spectrometry, spatial multi-omics, and functional biosensors, noting they enable co-registration of metabolite exposure with immune-cell states in human tumors.

It cites examples of intratumoral metabolite quantification in specific contexts, such as higher intra-tumoral/plasma TMAO associating with activated immune microenvironment in triple-negative breast cancer patients responding to immunotherapy.

It distinguishes between quantification in fecal/plasma samples (common) versus intratumoral samples (rare/challenging), highlighting the low-biomass and contamination risks associated with tumor tissue analysis.
